name: Dr Dray
shortDescription: A board-certified dermatologist answering skincare questions at length, ingredient by ingredient, including which trends are not worth the money.
longDescription: Five thousand uploads and a median around fifteen minutes, with eleven of the fifty most recent running over twenty. The subject is dermatology rather than beauty: how often exfoliation is actually warranted, one acid compared against another for a stated purpose, whether a drug prescribed for acne affects collagen, what a new ingredient with a marketing acronym does and whether it is worth the hype. She also covers the boundary between skin and the rest of medicine — skin signs that indicate something systemic, whether diet affects inflammation, what GLP-1 drugs do to skin — which is where a dermatologist's training earns its keep over a reviewer's. Her channel description discloses affiliate participation across several programmes, and product recommendation is a constant thread.
notFor: Anyone with a condition that needs diagnosis — this is education, not assessment, and skin problems are the kind that reward being looked at in person. Also expect a lot of product discussion.

categories.why: Ingredients and claims assessed by someone trained to assess them, including the routine ones people over-do and the new ones that turn out to be marketing.
categories.evidence: Long-form on how often exfoliation is warranted, direct comparisons between anti-ageing acids, whether a common acne drug affects collagen, an assessment of a hyped new ingredient, and skin signs that indicate systemic problems.

entryVideo.title: How Often Should You Really Exfoliate Your Skin?
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The single most over-done step in most routines, answered by frequency and reason rather than by product — which is the shape of good advice here.

caveats: Affiliate participation is disclosed on the channel and product recommendation runs through the catalogue — treat any specific purchase suggestion accordingly. Enormous back catalogue with no structure, so arrive with a question rather than browsing.

name: Mama Doctor Jones (Dr. Danielle Jones)
shortDescription: A board-certified obstetrician-gynaecologist taking apart the hormone and fertility claims sold to women online.
longDescription: Thirteen of the fifty most recent uploads run over twenty minutes and several pass forty. The corrective work is the reason to watch: a direct treatment of fertility influencers making false hormonal claims, an explanation of why particular pregnancy restrictions exist and which are folklore, an analysis of a viral unassisted birth, and a long piece on women turned away by doctors twice before being taken seriously. That last strand matters — she is as willing to name where medicine fails women as where the internet does, which is what separates a credible corrective voice from a defensive one. She has also covered how purity culture shapes what people believe about their own bodies, and reviews dramatised medical scenes to explain what is actually happening.
notFor: Anyone seeking guidance on their own pregnancy or condition — this is education and commentary, never assessment. The format is often reaction and commentary rather than instruction.

categories.why: The counterweight this subject most needs — a specialist dismantling specific hormone and fertility claims, while also naming where conventional care genuinely fails people.
categories.evidence: A 21-minute treatment of fertility influencers making false hormonal claims, a 21-minute explanation of which pregnancy restrictions have a basis and which do not, a 26-minute account of a patient turned away twice, and long-form on how cultural framing shapes belief about the body.

entryVideo.title: Hormone Fertility Influencers Are Lying to You (Again)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Names the specific claims and shows why they fail, which inoculates against a whole category of content rather than correcting one instance of it.

caveats: Largely corrective and commentary-shaped: you will learn what is false more often than what to do. Reaction to media and viral cases is a large part of the format, and the register is deliberately entertaining.
